outline.chapter_title: Technical Setting, Patents, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the radio-frequency interference problem that underlies the case, the two Finesse patents, the accused Nokia PIM-cancellation feature used by AT&T, and the litigation path from jury verdict to Federal Circuit appeal. It gives students the factual and procedural foundation needed to understand why the infringement disputes turned on highly specific signal-processing evidence.
subtopics: What intermodulation products (IMPs) are and how they arise when transmit signals interact with non-linear obstacles
The distinction between passive intermodulation (PIM), internal PIM, and external PIM
The basic objective of the asserted patents: mitigating IMP/PIM interference in radios
The parties and their roles: Finesse as patent owner, AT&T as accused infringer, Nokia as intervenor and supplier of the accused radios
The asserted patents and claims: claims 1–3 of the ’134 patent and claims 1, 4, 9, 16, 21, 29, and 36 of the ’775 patent
The accused functionality: Nokia radios’ PIM cancellation (PIM-C) feature
The trial result: jury findings of validity and infringement and a lump-sum damages award of $166,303,391
The post-trial motions: JMOL of noninfringement, JMOL on damages, and a new trial on damages
The appeal to the Federal Circuit and the two main appellate subjects: infringement sufficiency and damages

outline.chapter_title: The Appellate Framework: JMOL, Substantial Evidence, Claim Construction, and Proof of Infringement
outline.description: This chapter explains the standards of review and evidentiary principles that controlled the appeal. The opinion is a strong example of how patent law issues can be resolved through ordinary civil-review standards, especially when infringement depends on whether expert testimony actually supplies a coherent, limitation-by-limitation mapping to the accused technology.
subtopics: Why the Federal Circuit applied Fifth Circuit law to review the denial of JMOL and the denial of a new trial
The de novo standard for reviewing denial of JMOL under Fifth Circuit law
The substantial-evidence standard for a jury finding of infringement
The burden on the patentee to prove that every claim limitation is met by the accused product or method
De novo review of claim construction and clear-error review for any subsidiary factual findings
The practical importance of expert testimony in patent infringement cases involving technical diagrams and internal system documents
The line between permissible inference and impermissible reconstruction of a party’s proof after trial
How self-contradictory expert testimony can fail as a matter of law even when a jury found infringement
The court’s use of precedent, especially Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope, to assess contradictory testimony

outline.chapter_title: The ’134 Patent: Why Finesse Failed to Prove Sampling of Both Claimed Signal Types
outline.description: This chapter walks through the Federal Circuit’s reversal on the ’134 patent. The core issue was whether Finesse proved that the accused radios sampled a passband containing both the claimed 'signals of interest' and the claimed 'interference generating signals.' The court held that Finesse’s expert never provided a clear, non-contradictory mapping that could support the verdict.
subtopics: What the ’134 patent claims generally: reducing IMP interference by isolating signal categories and cancelling estimated interference
Representative claim 1 and the central role of limitation 1[a]
The requirement that the receiver over-sample a passband of received signals that includes both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals'
Dr. Wells’s trial theory based on a Nokia technical document showing the RF ADC, DL(TX) reference, modeled PIM path, and the red signal path
His express mapping of 'signals of interest' to the DL(TX) reference
His express mapping of 'interference generating signals' to the modeled PIM path
The critical technical problem exposed on cross-examination: the modeled PIM path is generated downstream of the RF ADC and therefore cannot be sampled by the RF ADC before it exists
Dr. Wells’s attempted pivot to 'x1' and 'x2' as two signals on the red path
Why the Federal Circuit found the pivot inadequate: he never clearly mapped x1 and x2 onto the claim’s required signal categories
The district court’s view that Dr. Wells was 'clearly referring to x1 and x2' and why the Federal Circuit rejected that reading
The court’s refusal to accept Finesse’s appellate effort to reconstruct a clearer theory from scattered portions of the record
The role of self-contradictory expert testimony in the court’s insufficiency analysis
Application of Johns Hopkins: when the party with the burden relies on contradictory expert testimony, no reasonable jury need credit the theory
The result for the ’134 patent: reversal of the denial of JMOL of noninfringement because substantial evidence did not support the verdict

outline.chapter_title: The ’775 Patent: Claim Scope, Prosecution History, and the Failure to Prove Seven Claimed Multiplications
outline.description: This chapter explains the two distinct issues presented by the ’775 patent: first, whether the claims were limited to three unique input signals; and second, whether the accused radios were shown to perform the seven specified multiplications. The Federal Circuit rejected the defendants’ narrowing claim-scope argument but still found noninfringement because Finesse’s proof did not establish the actual multiplication limitation.
subtopics: What the ’775 patent claims generally: digital generation of IMP cancellation signals in a co-located transmitter/receiver system
Representative claim 1 and its structure, including the requirement of generating ICSs using 'three signals S1, S2 and S3'
The detailed multiplication limitation: seven third-order products listed in claim 1[d]
The district court’s summary-judgment construction that 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' must be 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique'
The intrinsic and extrinsic evidence the district court relied on, including inventor testimony
Appellants’ waiver issue in the district court regarding any late attempt to require three unique signals
The prosecution-history argument on appeal: amendment from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' to overcome Filipovic
Why the Federal Circuit found no clear and unambiguous disavowal of systems using only two unique inputs
The court’s reading of the amendment as requiring three separately identifiable signals rather than a fixed number of unique inputs
Dr. Wells’s infringement theory using a Nokia document to equate the accused operations with the claim’s seven multiplications
The technical mismatch identified by the Federal Circuit: the document showed modulus and complex-conjugate operations rather than the seven claimed products
The document’s disclosure of only three distinct multiplications: x1·|x1|·|x1|, x1·x1·x2', and x1·|x2|·|x2|
Why three distinct multiplications could not satisfy a claim expressly requiring seven listed multiplications absent evidence that all seven were performed
The absence of trial testimony clearly mapping the three accused operations onto each of the seven claimed products
Why Finesse’s appellate clarifications could not cure deficiencies in the trial record
The additional flaw in Finesse’s mapping: treating S3 as though it could simultaneously correspond to x2, x2', and |x2|
The oral-argument contention that Nokia documents showed ten multiplications, and why that too failed without a supported subset-to-claim mapping
The result for the ’775 patent: reversal of the denial of JMOL of noninfringement for lack of substantial evidence

outline.chapter_title: Disposition, Damages, and the Case’s Litigation Lessons
outline.description: This final chapter ties together the court’s remedial rulings and explains the opinion’s broader significance for patent-litigation practice. The case illustrates the difference between winning a claim-construction dispute and actually proving infringement, as well as the danger of relying on expert testimony that is internally inconsistent or only becomes coherent through post-trial advocacy.
subtopics: Why the damages rulings did not survive once liability was undone
The standard of review for denial of a new trial on damages under Fifth Circuit law
The court’s choice to vacate the damages award rather than reach the merits of the damages challenge
The formal disposition: reversed and vacated, with costs to defendants-appellants
How the opinion separates claim-scope questions from evidentiary sufficiency questions
The lesson that even a patentee-favorable construction does not relieve the patentee of proving each express limitation with record evidence
The importance of precise limitation-by-limitation mapping from technical documents to claim language
Why post hoc explanations by counsel cannot substitute for what the expert actually told the jury
The case as a warning about contradictory expert testimony in complex patent cases
The opinion’s significance for future JMOL motions in cases built on technical schematics and expert interpretation
